item.title: Radiolab: More Perfect: Cruel and Unusual
item.description:
This week, we’re replaying the inaugural episode of More Perfect (first aired in 2016) we explore three little words embedded in the 8th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution: “cruel and unusual.” America has long wrestled with this concept in the context of our strongest punishment, the death penalty. A majority of “we the people” (61 percent, to be exact) are in favor of having it, but inside the Supreme Court, opinions have evolved over time in surprising ways.

And outside of the court, the debate drove one woman in the UK to take on the U.S. death penalty system from Europe. It also caused states to resuscitate old methods used for executing prisoners on death row. And perhaps more than anything, it forced a conversation on what constitutes cruel and unusual punishment.

In this episode, we also include a new conversation with Harvard law professor Carol Steiker and former death-row inmate Damien Nichols about the moment the death penalty finds itself in now. After the botched execution of Christa Pike, and with the government considering livestreaming a firing squad execution, how do we understand the death penalty in 2026?

Special thanks to Claire Phillips, Nina Perry, Stephanie Jenkins, Ralph Dellapiana, Byrd Pinkerton, Elisabeth Semel, Christina Spaulding, Carol Steiker, Damien Nichols, and The Marshall Project

item.title: Freakonomics Radio: 694. Does Democracy Really Need Elections?
item.description:
Stephen Dubner recently served on a criminal jury. Twelve strangers — selected randomly and barely paid — took the job seriously. Afterward, he wondered: why can’t our politics work that way? A growing movement, inspired by Athenian democracy, says it can.

    • Terry Bouricius, author and former Vermont state representative.
    • Dj Hairston, public-defense lawyer.

    • Hélène Landemore, professor of political science at Yale University.

item.title: The Automation Ladies: You Are Either A Risk Or An Investment with Bill Seaman
item.description:
Most manufacturing hiring advice is either vague or completely detached from how industrial automation jobs really work. So I brought on Bill Seaman, Director of People Operations at Philomatic, to get brutally practical about what attracts great engineers, technicians, and field service talent and what quietly drives them away.

We start with the reality a lot of people avoid talking about: layoffs, short tenures, and career pivots. Bill explains how candidates can reframe those moments, show adaptability, and answer the unspoken question every hiring manager has: are you a risk or an investment? From there, we dig into career growth inside OEMs and machine builders, including why companies need strong individual contributor paths (senior and principal roles) instead of forcing great technical people into people management.

Then we get into the hiring mechanics that matter. We break down job descriptions and bias, why bloated “nice-to-have” requirements shrink your applicant pool, and how interview structure can improve both candidate experience and team buy-in. We also cover diversity in manufacturing, visa sponsorship and OPT timelines, and the hidden retention killer many long-tenured companies face: salary compression and outdated pay bands. To round it out, Bill shares benefits that compete when you cannot outspend bigger companies, like real flexibility, schedule options, and creative wellness support.

If you’re hiring in industrial automation or trying to land your next role, you’ll walk away with a clearer playbook. Subscribe, share this with a teammate, and leave us a review with the most outdated hiring rule you want to see disappear.

item.title: Hyperfixed: How America Got Online
item.description:
This week, a story made in partnership with 99% Invisible and The BBC as part of their project A History of the United States in 100 Objects. 

When Jan Brandt joined the marketing team of fledgling internet company America Online in 1993, she had to figure out how to sell a service that most people in the US had no idea how to use -- the internet. We talk to her about how she managed to use a small, unbiquitous physical object to help steer their virtual service toward the biggest corporate merger in history.

item.title: Ignited: Striking Industrial Automation Conversations: From Alarm to Action: Turning Incident Response into Operational Intelligence
item.description:
Most industrial operations have alarms, but far fewer have a standardized approach for what happens next when an incident occurs. Between detection and resolution, response workflows frequently break down—leading to unclear ownership, misdirected alerts, and recurring issues. In this episode, Travis and Tom sit down with Brooks Korfhage and Celine Mbanasor from IGear to discuss turning alarms from noise into structured action. They explore how pairing Ignition with IGear's SQUEAKS platform orchestrates incident response, matches the right responder to the right issue, and turns real-time operational data into continuous improvement insights.

item.title: Planet Money: The history of light (classic)
item.description:
How do you measure human progress? Light is the answer.

For thousands of years, getting light was a huge hassle. You had to make candles from scratch. This is not as romantic as it sounds. You had to get a cow, raise the cow, feed the cow, kill the cow, get the fat out of the cow, cook the fat, dip wicks into the fat. All that — for not very much light. Now, if we want to light a whole room, we just flip a switch.

Nobel-winning economist Bill Nordhaus passed away last week. He was known for his work on the economics of climate change, but he also came up with this idea that the history of light explains reveals why the world today is the way it is. It explains why we aren't all subsistence farmers, and why we can afford to have artists and massage therapists and plumbers. (And, yes, people who make podcasts about the history of light.) The history of light is the history of economic growth — of things getting faster, cheaper, and more efficient. It shows us the pie can get bigger, sometimes, there can be a type of progress where everyone is better off. 

On today's show, one of our all time favorites: How we got from dim little candles made out of cow fat, to as much light as we want at the flick of a switch, and how that is a measure of what economic progress means. 

(Note: This episode originally ran in 2014.)

item.title: Manufacturing Happy Hour: 309: How Physical AI Is Changing What's Possible in Warehouse Automation
item.description:
In a factory, work in progress is a problem. In a warehouse, it’s the whole job.

Chris takes the show inside the warehouse with Josh Cloer, General Manager, North America at Nomagic, and Onur Uranli, Director, Enterprise Business Development & Strategic Growth at Intelligrated. It’s an adjacent topic, but every product a factory makes ends up in one.

Josh, back after first joining the show in 2022, explains what physical AI means for a robot that must work out what went wrong. Onur asks whether the pallets arriving at a warehouse are ready for the automation built to receive them. Together they look at why warehouses are playing catch-up with factories, and why the answer starts with Henry Ford.

In this episode, find out:

  • Why most warehouses are still manual, and where automation investment has gone so far
  • What the “forgotten middle” of warehouse automation looks like
  • How physical AI helps a robot work out what went wrong and recover from downtime
  • Why the same item can look different by the time it reaches the warehouse
  • Where warehouse automation is catching up to the factory, and what each side can learn from the other
  • How MHI’s Robotics Group helps automation vendors work together

item.title: NerdWallet's Smart Money Podcast: HMO, PPO or High-Deductible Plan? Navigate Open Enrollment as Health Care Costs Rise
item.description:
Learn how to compare health insurance plans, HSAs and FSAs before open enrollment deadlines arrive.
How do you pick the right health plan when costs keep climbing? Hosts Sean Pyles, CFP®, and Elizabeth Ayoola kick off a two-part open enrollment series with NerdWallet lead writer Kate Ashford, starting with the key enrollment dates for marketplace, Medicare, federal and employer-sponsored coverage. They discuss why employer health benefit costs are expected to jump next year, how premiums and deductibles work like a seesaw, the tradeoffs between HMOs, PPOs and high-deductible health plans, and why being a middle-of-the-road health care user could make the choice especially tricky. You’ll also hear how to weigh your out-of-pocket maximum, whether you have enough cash on hand to cover a high deductible, and how last year’s medical bills could help you estimate next year’s.
How can you get the most out of a health savings account or flexible spending account? Sean, Elizabeth and Kate explain the triple tax advantage of HSAs and why some planners treat them like another retirement account, how use-it-or-lose-it rules and rollover limits work for FSAs, and what a dependent care FSA could cover. They also dig into what’s changing for Affordable Care Act plans in 2027, including higher proposed premiums, insurers entering and leaving markets, new subsidy eligibility rules for some immigrants and state-level changes, plus why it could be worth trying to negotiate a medical bill.

item.title: Filmspotting: The Third Man vs. Touch of Evil with Matt Gourley and Anne Thompson | Movie Death Match
item.description:
For our Noirvember edition, Chris Klimek convenes a showdown between two noir classics featuring unforgettable Orson Welles villains: Carol Reed's The Third Man and Welles's own Touch of Evil.

One is a postwar mystery set amid the shattered streets and shadows of occupied Vienna, featuring Welles as the charmingly monstrous Harry Lime. The other is a feverish border-town nightmare with the filmmaker buried beneath prosthetics as corrupt police captain Hank Quinlan.

Arguing for The Third Man is Matt Gourley (Conan O'Brien Needs a Friend, With Gourley and Rust, James Bonding), who contends that Reed's masterpiece transcends noir, combining unforgettable atmosphere, moral ambiguity, and one of cinema's greatest endings. Representing Touch of Evil is Anne Thompson (IndieWire, Screen Talk), who makes the case that Welles's final Hollywood film is a singular feat of visual storytelling and one of the boldest achievements ever produced within the studio system.

Which Welles villain casts the longer shadow, and which film deserves to survive? Choose your winner at moviedeathmatch.com.
